notes.headline: Palo Alto Networks: next-generation ARR up 66%, guidance ‘materially’ raised, and a move into AI models
notes.takeaway: Revenue grew 39% to $3.44 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.05 beat the $0.97 consensus, but the figure that moved the stock 17% was next-generation security ARR of $9.73 billion, up 66%. Management raised full-year guidance and announced it intends to buy Applied Compute, a platform for running open-weight AI models.
results: Palo Alto Networks reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $3.44 billion, up 39% from $2.47 billion a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were $1.05 against a consensus of about $0.97 and $0.93 a year ago. Reported net income was $482 million, or $0.57 per share.

Next-generation security annual recurring revenue reached $9.73 billion, up 66%, and remaining performance obligations — contracted revenue not yet recognised — grew 35% to $21.0 billion. Adjusted operating income was $1.1 billion against $746 million a year earlier. Reported operating income fell to $96 million from $309 million, reflecting acquisition-related and share-based costs.

Adjusted free cash flow was $1.9 billion, a 56.2% margin for the quarter. The first quarter is seasonally the strongest for cash collection, and the company guides to 38.0% for the full year, so the quarterly figure should not be annualised.
mgmt: Chief executive Nikesh Arora called it a record first quarter with one of the company’s largest ever beats on next-generation ARR, and tied demand to what he described as an unprecedented threat environment as AI changes how attacks are carried out.

Chief financial officer Dipak Golechha said the company was ‘materially raising’ full-year guidance after acceleration across each segment in what is normally a seasonally slower quarter. For fiscal 2027 the company now expects revenue of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion (growth of 26% to 27%), next-generation ARR of $11.475 billion to $11.525 billion, adjusted EPS of $4.26 to $4.30 and an adjusted operating margin of 29.5%.

For the second quarter it expects revenue of $3.53 billion to $3.55 billion, up 36% to 37%, and adjusted EPS of $1.01 to $1.03. The company also announced its intent to acquire Applied Compute, which it says will let it deliver secure open-weight AI models to customers.
view: The 66% growth in next-generation ARR needs one qualification before it is celebrated: part of it is acquired. Palo Alto has been buying its way into adjacent categories, and the year-over-year comparison includes businesses that were not in the base a year ago. That does not make the number false, but it means the organic growth rate is lower than the headline, and the full-year guide — ARR growth of 26% to 27% — is the better indication of the underlying pace once acquisitions are lapped.

What is genuinely strong is the direction of travel in the platform strategy. Palo Alto’s bet has been that customers will consolidate a dozen security vendors into one, accepting a single supplier in exchange for integration. Remaining performance obligations of $21 billion growing 35% say customers are signing larger, longer commitments, which is exactly what consolidation looks like in the numbers. A security vendor with that much contracted revenue has unusual visibility for a software company.

The gap between reported and adjusted profit is the thing to watch rather than wave away. Adjusted operating income rose to $1.1 billion while reported operating income fell to $96 million. The difference is share-based compensation and acquisition costs, and both are real: one dilutes shareholders, the other is the cost of the growth being reported. A company that grows by acquisition and pays heavily in stock will always look better on the adjusted line, and the diluted share count in the guidance — 844 to 847 million — is the honest measure of what each holder owns.

The Applied Compute deal is a strategic statement more than a financial one. Palo Alto is positioning itself not only as the company that secures AI but as one that supplies the models enterprises run, which is a larger and more contested market than security. It could be far-sighted, or it could be a security company wandering from what it is best at. After a 17% move on the day, the shares price in the raised guidance fully; the next two quarters have to show the acceleration was demand rather than deal timing.
notes.watch: Organic next-generation ARR growth once the acquired businesses are in the base, and the gap between adjusted and reported operating income. The first tells you how fast the platform is really growing; the second tells you what that growth costs shareholders.
